title: Adversarial Attacks of Vision Tasks in the Past 10 Years: A Survey
evidence_quote: Evasion attacks occur during inference, where subtle input perturbations mislead the model into incorrect outputs.
notes: 10-year survey of visual adversarial examples plus LVLM attacks. Core studied harm is misclassification of image input (wrong final prediction, no signal). The LVLM chapter also covers prompt injection/jailbreak (goal-hijack), so consequence is a dominance call.

title: Context-Aware RL for Agentic and Multimodal LLMs
evidence_quote: We refer to it as context unawareness: the relevant information is available in the context, yet the model's prediction is not grounded in it.
notes: Genuinely two channels: 1k contrastive contexts are coding-agent trajectories/tool traces (tool-output) and 7K are images (cross-modal); 12 VQA vs 5 agentic benchmarks tips it to cross-modal. Consequence also split: VQA misreads = wrong final answer, code edit removing a variable = intermediate decision.

title: Enhancing Security in LLM Applications: A Performance Evaluation of Early Detection Systems
evidence_quote: In prompt leakage attacks, an attacker maliciously manipulates the LLM into outputting its system instructions, violating the system's confidentiality.
notes: Evaluates LLM Guard, Vigil, Rebuff on prompt-leak detection. Paper states 'The prompt injection resides in a user prompt', so the route is direct-input, not tool-output.

title: Whispers of Wealth: Red-Teaming Google's Agent Payments Protocol via Prompt Injection
evidence_quote: Branded Whisper Attack: an indirect prompt injection attack in which adversarial instructions embedded in product descriptions manipulate ranking decisions.
notes: Product descriptions reach the Shopping Agent as the Merchant Agent's A2A response, so route is multi-agent; tool-output is a defensible alternative. Second attack (Vault Whisper) is direct-input/data-exfiltration at 20% ASR vs 100% for the ranking attack, so the ranking attack dominates. Not resource-abuse: the harm measured is ranking manipulation, not spend on the attacker's behalf.

title: WAB: Overcoming Memory, Network, and Security Walls in Native Agentic Browsers with WebAssembly
evidence_quote: A malicious page can trick the agent into risky side effects (e.g., unintended external requests) unless the runtime enforces least-privilege actions with explicit, revocable authority.
notes: 4-page WWW companion PoC. Security wall (prompt injection from untrusted web pages fetched by the browser agent) is one of three walls; the other two (memory, network) are non-adversarial context/latency management, hence Both.

title: SafeSearch: Automated Red-Teaming of LLM-Based Search Agents
evidence_quote: When benign queries retrieve unreliable search results, we study how agents incorporate and propagate them in their final responses, exposing risks such as harmful output (Zou et al., 2025), indirect prompt injection (Perez & Ribeiro, 2022), advertisement promotion (Nestaas et al., 2025)
notes: Search results returned by a search tool (coded tool-output rather than RAG; the agent calls a search engine, not a corpus retriever). Consequence is a dominance call: the measured harm is unsafe/unreliable content propagated into the agent's final response under a benign query, but one of five risk categories is indirect prompt injection (goal-hijack).

title: Small Models, Big Tasks: An Exploratory Empirical Study on Small Language Models for Function Calling
evidence_quote: Prompt injection refers to the manipulation of the user prompt to alter the output of the generative model [33]. This involves appending certain special characters, instructions, or adversarial text to the initial prompt leading to toxic, biased, and undesirable outputs.
notes: Mainly a capability study of small LMs for function calling; the injection arm ('with and without prompt injection', 'robustness to minor perturbations in the user prompt') is a genuine but minor adversarial component, hence Both rather than Security. Harm measured is degraded function-call generation (an intermediate action), not a wrong final answer.

title: The Convergent Cyber Threat Horizon in Financial Services: Artificial Intelligence, Agentic Systems, Deepfakes, Quantum Computing, and the Mythos of Large Language Models
evidence_quote: An agent that ingests external content is exposed to adversarial instructions embedded in that content [28]. Indirect prompt injection is the OWASP LLM01 top risk for 2025 [29] and has no fully general defence
notes: Sector-wide threat-landscape review (finance) covering five forces: generative AI, agentic AI, deepfakes (cross-modal), quantum, and LLM 'mythos'. Only one of ten listed threat surfaces is context-integrity relevant; it names 'indirect prompt injection via retrieved content'. Single-channel coding is forced; low confidence.

title: VATS: Exploiting Implicit Authority in Error-Path Injection via Systematic Mutation
evidence_quote: adversarial instructions in tool outputs that redirect agent behavior (Greshake et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2026; Zhan et al., 2024). Because of a fundamental trust-authorization mismatch, tool-stream content routinely bypasses text-level safety alignments
notes: Error-path injection is a sub-channel of tool-output (the tool's error return), not tool-metadata; the paper explicitly contrasts it with 'standard tool-response IPI'. Up to 100% compliance with attacker-supplied recovery steps.

title: Can Retrieval Heads See Images? Multimodal Retrieval Heads in Long-Context Vision-Language Models
evidence_quote: selected heads drops MMLongBench-Doc from 48.2% to 5.7% and SlideVQA from 71.2% to 8.9%, while random-head masking is far less damaging
notes: Mechanistic study of multimodal retrieval heads over long interleaved text-image contexts with distractors. Measured harm is downstream QA accuracy (wrong final answer). Ablation also makes models 'explicitly state that the needed context is missing' (a refusal, i.e. availability-loss), but that is secondary.

title: AgentSecBench: Measuring Prompt Injection, Privacy Leakage, and Tool-Use Integrity in LLM Agents
evidence_quote: In the retrieval-confidentiality game, a context contains a secret assigned to a tenant outside the caller's authorization scope
notes: Three games span three channels: a document carrying an adversarial instruction, a retrieved context carrying an out-of-scope secret, and a tool observation naming a forbidden action (tool-output). Coded RAG because two of three games route through retrieved documents/context and the paper reports a 'RAG leakage' estimator. Consequence also split between canary disclosure and forbidden-capability selection (goal-hijack).

title: Trojan's Whisper: Stealthy Manipulation of OpenClaw through Injected Bootstrapped Guidance
evidence_quote: guidance injection manipulates the agent's reasoning context by framing harmful actions as routine best practices. These narratives are automatically incorporated into the agent's interpretive framework and influence future task execution without raising suspicion.
notes: Third-party skills injecting bootstrap guidance files, so channel is skill (not direct-input). Consequence is a judgement call: the vector is inherently persistent (guidance reloads every session) and 'persistent backdoor installation' is one of 13 attack categories, but what is measured is ASR of attacker-chosen harmful actions (16.0-64.2%) executed autonomously, which is goal-hijack.

title: An Early Categorization of Prompt Injection Attacks on Large Language Models
evidence_quote: in a prompt injection, the attacker attempts to get a chatbot or an LLM assisted tool to take some undesired action or produce some malicious output through creative formatting of the input (prompt) given to the model
notes: Early (2024) categorization paper, mostly direct user-side injection/jailbreaking, with indirect injection via browser/email plugins mentioned as an emerging extension. Prompt leaking is one of the categories, so data-exfiltration is a secondary fit.

title: MAGIC: A Multi-Hop and Graph-Based Benchmark for Inter-Context Conflicts in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
evidence_quote: both open-source and proprietary models struggle with conflict detection—especially when multi-hop reasoning is required—and often fail to pinpoint the exact source of contradictions
notes: Benchmark of inter-context knowledge conflict among retrieved documents; no adversary. The benchmark's task is conflict detection, so a missed conflict is a wrong final answer under misleading context.

title: MemGym: a Long-Horizon Memory Environment for LLM Agents
evidence_quote: LLM agents operating over long horizons must continuously decide what to preserve, summarize, or evict as observations, tool outputs, and intermediate conclusions accumulate.
notes: Memory benchmark with memory-isolated scoring that deliberately decouples memory failures from end-task success, so the measured harm is the quality of intermediate preserve/evict/compress decisions rather than a final answer.

title: Soft Begging: Modular and Efficient Shielding of LLMs against Prompt Injection and Jailbreaking based on Prompt Tuning
evidence_quote: Dangers of prompt injections include data leakage, i.e., the disclosure of sensitive information, and system manipulation, i.e., altering the behaviour of the system based on the injected prompt. In the most extreme case, the adversarial user can hijack the LLM
notes: Two-page extended abstract proposing 'soft begging' (soft-prompt tuning) as a shield. Covers jailbreaking plus direct AND indirect prompt injection without committing to one setting; coded direct-input because the defence operates on the corrupted prompt and jailbreaking is the running example. Data leakage is a co-equal stated danger.

title: AgenticOS: An Intent-Oriented Secure Operating System Architecture for Autonomous AI Agents
evidence_quote: Once an agent runtime is compromised by prompt injection, supply-chain poisoning, or malicious tool outputs, an attacker may combine these primitives into behaviors far beyond the scope of the user's task authorization.
notes: OS-architecture proposal (capability isolation, intent ABI); deliberately channel-agnostic, naming prompt injection, supply-chain poisoning and malicious tool outputs together. No empirical evaluation of a specific channel, so the single-channel pick is weak. Exfiltration and persistence are also named as downstream effects.

title: HarmfulSkillBench: How Do Harmful Skills Weaponize Your Agents?
evidence_quote: presenting a harmful task through a pre-installed skill substantially lowers refusal rates across all models, with the average harm score rising from 0.27 without the skill to 0.47 with it, and further to 0.76 when the harmful intent is implicit rather than stated as an explicit user request
notes: Measurement of 98,440 public skills plus a benchmark; adversary is the harmful-skill builder. Strongest condition is the implicit-intent one, where the skill rather than the user supplies the objective, which is why goal-hijack fits better than a pure jailbreak/safety-bypass reading.

title: ADEMA: A Knowledge-State Orchestration Architecture for Long-Horizon Knowledge Synthesis with LLMAgents
evidence_quote: Long-horizon LLM tasks often fail not because a single answer is unattainable, but because knowledge states drift across rounds, intermediate commitments remain implicit, and interruption fractures the evolving evidence chain.
notes: Architecture paper; the accumulating context is the agent's own condensed memory, checkpoints and artifact lineage across rounds, hence memory rather than direct-input. Note the headline experimental result is that removing checkpoint/resume produced the only INVALID run, which is an availability-loss signal; reasoning-corruption is coded from the paper's stated failure model (knowledge-state drift).

title: Episodic-Semantic Memory Architecture for Long-Horizon Scientific Agents
evidence_quote: while full-context models fail at 10,000 messages due to context overflow, our system maintains 70–85% accuracy with 1–2 second latency using 62% fewer tokens (45,434 vs 120,000+ limit)
notes: Problem statement is 'context window saturation has emerged as a critical bottleneck'; the headline baseline failure is outright context overflow, i.e. the agent cannot finish at all. QA accuracy across 1,440 queries (silent-corruption) is the secondary measure, so this is a defensible but not certain availability-loss.

title: Drift No More? Context Equilibria in Multi-Turn LLM Interactions
evidence_quote: A recurring challenge in this setting is context drift: the gradual divergence of a model's outputs from goal-consistent behavior across turns
notes: Drift is measured as turn-wise KL divergence from a goal-consistent reference policy, i.e. degraded behaviour across turns rather than one wrong final answer. No adversary. Conversation history is the degrading context.

title: Follow My Instruction and Spill the Beans: Scalable Data Extraction from Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
evidence_quote: an adversary can exploit the instruction-following capability of LMs (Brown et al., 2020) to reconstruct datastore content by explicitly prompting LMs to repeat the context (Prompt-Injected Data Extraction)
notes: Coded by the route rule: the attacker is a black-box API user whose payload enters via the query, so the channel is direct-input; the RAG datastore is the ASSET being extracted, not the route. If the project convention is to code the compromised asset, this would be RAG instead - flagging for the validator. 100% leakage success on 25 customized GPTs.

title: Cybersecurity AI: Hacking the AI Hackers via Prompt Injection
evidence_quote: When AI agents designed to find and exploit vulnerabilities interact with malicious web servers, carefully crafted reponses can hijack their execution flow, potentially granting attackers system access.
notes: Payload lives in the HTTP response the pentest agent's scanning tool returns. 100% exploitation across 14 attack variants; defense reduces to 0%.

title: SING: Synthetic Intention Graph for Scalable Active Tool Discovery in LLM Agents
evidence_quote: Exposing hundreds or thousands of schemas consumes substantial context budget, introduces many irrelevant tools, and can weaken the model's retention of task-critical information
notes: No adversary; the degrading content is bulk tool schemas/descriptions read before calling. Measured harm is tool-retrieval Recall@5 and downstream success, i.e. wrong intermediate tool-selection decisions. Context-budget exhaustion is named as a cause, so availability-loss is a weaker alternative.

title: Fun-tuning: Characterizing the Vulnerability of Proprietary LLMs to Optimization-Based Prompt Injection Attacks via the Fine-Tuning Interface
evidence_quote: An attacker could craft an adversarial prompt and send an unsolicited email to a victim user. If the user asks their email-handling agent to "summarize my latest email," the adversarial prompt will hijack the agent and cause it to also send out the user's emails to the attacker
notes: The novelty is the optimization oracle (Gemini fine-tuning loss), not the delivery route; the paper's canonical deployment is content the agent fetches (email), and evaluation uses the PurpleLlama prompt-injection benchmark. The motivating example ends in exfiltration, but the measured outcome is the model obeying injected instructions (65-82% ASR).

title: Human-Interpretable Adversarial Prompt Attack on Large Language Models with Situational Context
evidence_quote: The full prompt attack was designed to have a combination of a malicious prompt, an adversarial insertion, and a situation that can force a model to generate undesirable/unsafe responses.
notes: Optimization-free jailbreak: attacker submits the whole prompt template (malicious request + human-readable adversarial insertion + movie situational context) directly to the chat interface. Closer to jailbreaking than to classic injection, but goal-hijack is the only fitting consequence.

title: Disrupting Large Language Models with Hidden Prompt Injection Attacks Embedded in HTML Pages
evidence_quote: Our investigation subjects LLMs to rigorous testing using HTML pages containing concealed instructions designed to terminate response generation when users make queries.
notes: Channel changed from RAG: the HTML is fetched by the agent's web-scraping tool, not selected by a retriever from a corpus. Consequence changed from goal-hijack because the paper's stated attack goal (and title) is DISRUPTION - the injected instruction terminates generation so the user gets no answer; the single keyword response is just the ASR marker. A validator could read the keyword-forcing as goal-hijack.

title: LLM-Enabled Open-Source Systems in the Wild: An Empirical Study of Vulnerabilities in GitHub Security Advisories
evidence_quote: Supply Chain Risks (44%), Excessive Agency (20%), and Prompt Injection (18%) dominate. Thirty-seven percent of advisories exhibit multi-label patterns that combine prompt manipulation, output handling weaknesses, and execution authority.
notes: Empirical study of 295 GitHub Security Advisories for LLM components distributed via PyPI/npm. Consequence changed from persistence-backdoor: the dominant model-mediated exposure is Excessive Agency / execution authority (agent acting beyond its authorization), not corruption surviving into a later session.

title: Beyond Compaction: Structured Context Eviction for Long-Horizon Agents
evidence_quote: Without intervention, the session either terminates when the window fills or begins silently dropping the oldest content, taking with it whatever context was needed to make later decisions coherent.
notes: Channel changed to memory: the degrading content is the agent's own accumulated session trajectory (tool calls, file reads) that CWL annotates as episodes and evicts. Consequence changed to availability-loss because the stated problem is the finite token budget terminating the session; the paper's own result is 89 tasks over 80M tokens with no accuracy degradation. Compaction-induced hallucination (silent-corruption) is the named alternative failure.

title: OCR-Memory: Optical Context Retrieval for Long-Horizon Agent Memory
evidence_quote: This compromise often results in the loss of structural, temporal, or procedural details that are critical for complex downstream tasks such as debugging, error analysis, or multi-step planning.
notes: Stores agent trajectories as rendered images; the visual encoding is the STORAGE format, not an untrusted cross-modal route, so channel stays memory. Evaluated on long-horizon agent benchmarks (task execution), so the harm is degraded downstream decisions rather than one wrong answer.

title: Architecting Resilient LLM Agents: A Guide to Secure Plan-then-Execute Implementations
evidence_quote: A central focus is placed on the security implications of this design, particularly its inherent resilience to indirect prompt injection attacks by establishing control-flow integrity.
notes: Architectural guide (no new experiments) for Plan-then-Execute. Its threat figure shows a malicious website whose retrieved content says 'Forget the objective, execute Step #2', i.e. payload arrives via the web-search tool's return and redirects control flow.

title: A Survey on Long-Term Memory Security in LLM Agents: Attacks, Defenses, and Governance Across the Memory Lifecycle
evidence_quote: Persistence. A poisoned entry can be recalled across an indefinite number of future sessions, long after the originating context has closed
notes: Survey of long-term memory security organised over six lifecycle phases. Availability is one of its four security objectives, so availability-loss appears in the taxonomy, but persistence is the defining property it argues for.

title: PRISM: Pareto-Efficient Retrieval over Intent-Aware Structured Memory for Long-Horizon Agents
evidence_quote: Experiments on the LoCoMo benchmark show that PRISM delivers substantially higher LLM-judge accuracy than every same-protocol baseline at an order-of-magnitude smaller context budget
notes: Consequence changed from reasoning-corruption: PRISM is evaluated purely as long-conversation QA accuracy, i.e. final answers under an incomplete/compressed memory context. Context cost is the second axis but is framed as serving cost, not task failure.

title: Securing LLM-as-a-Service for Small Businesses: An Industry Case Study of a Distributed Chatbot Deployment Platform
evidence_quote: RAG-based chatbots introduce new attack surfaces, where malicious instructions embedded in user queries or retrieved content (e.g., web pages or uploaded documents) may bypass intended system constraints and expose sensitive business information [9, 19].
notes: Industry case study of a multi-tenant k3s chatbot platform. The stated harm is exposure of sensitive business information across tenant boundaries, hence data-exfiltration over goal-hijack. Channel is RAG (retrieved company documents); user queries are named as a co-equal route.

title: Beyond Entangled Planning: Task-Decoupled Planning for Long-Horizon Agents
evidence_quote: both paradigms suffer from entangled contexts, where the agent must reason over a monolithic history spanning multiple sub-tasks. This entanglement increases cognitive load and lets local errors propagate across otherwise independent decisions, making recovery computationally expensive.
notes: Channel changed from direct-input: the degrading content is the agent's own accumulated execution history across earlier turns, which TDP scopes per sub-task. Harm is error propagation across planning decisions (intermediate), plus an 82% token-cost reduction.

title: IterInject: Indirect Prompt Injection Against LLM Agents via Feedback-Guided Iterative Optimization
evidence_quote: adversarial instructions embedded in external data sources—emails, documents, web pages—can hijack agent behavior without direct interaction with the victim
notes: Evaluated on AgentDojo and InjectAgent (payload returned by tool calls) plus Claude Code. Clear indirect-injection hijack; no ambiguity on either axis.

title: AegisAgent: An Autonomous Defense Agent Against Prompt Injection Attacks in LLM-HARs
evidence_quote: Attackers inject adversarial manipulations in the sensor-to-prompt pathway, altering the generated descriptions and thereby misleading downstream LLM-based HAR models. This can lead to hazardous result in safety-critical applications, such as changing a fall result to be walking normally.
notes: Channel changed to cross-modal: IMU wearable-sensor signals are rendered into text descriptions and the attacker tampers with that conversion path; tool-output is the alternative reading if sensor reads are treated as tool returns. Consequence changed to silent-corruption: the measured harm is a wrong activity classification (a fall reported as normal walking) with nothing to flag it, not the agent pursuing a new objective.

title: Robust Pronoun Fidelity with English LLMs: Are they Reasoning, Repeating, or Just Biased?
evidence_quote: models are easily distracted by non-adversarial sentences discussing other people; even one sentence with a distractor pronoun causes accuracy to drop on average by 34 percentage points
notes: Explicitly non-adversarial distractors placed in the prompt context; 5M-instance dataset, 37 model variants. Harm measured is final pronoun-prediction accuracy.

title: MobileSafetyBench: Evaluating Safety of Autonomous Agents in Mobile Device Control
evidence_quote: After checking a message that contains a new malicious instruction, the agent sells the user's stock shares following the injected instruction.
notes: Mobile device-control benchmark; 50 of its high-risk tasks are indirect prompt injection, where 'a message containing the content is sent from a stranger' and the agent reads it as an app observation (coded tool-output; cross-modal is arguable since observations are screen-derived). The other 200 daily-scenario tasks are non-adversarial misuse/side-effect safety, so a Both reading is possible, but those are safety-harm rather than context degradation.

title: Practical Reasoning Interruption Attacks on Reasoning Large Language Models
evidence_quote: an adversary can prematurely terminate the model's reasoning process, causing it to deliver an empty final answer
notes: Consequence changed from reasoning-corruption: the attack's whole point is that the model stops and returns nothing usable (109-token payload exploiting 'reasoning token overflow') - capability is lost and the attacker gains nothing from the output itself. A secondary RTO application is a jailbreak that leaks reasoning tokens into the final answer, which would be goal-hijack.

title: CUB: Benchmarking Context Utilisation Techniques for Language Models
evidence_quote: the first comprehensive benchmark designed to help diagnose CMTs under diverse noisy context conditions within retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)
notes: Channel changed from direct-input: contexts are retrieved passages (gold, conflicting, irrelevant) in a RAG setting over NQ, DRUID and CounterFact. Consequence changed to silent-corruption: the benchmark scores final QA/fact-checking answers under misleading context. No adversary - conflicts arise from stale parametric memory and imperfect retrieval.

title: ReliabilityRAG: Effective and Provably Robust Defense for RAG-based Web-Search
evidence_quote: The retrieval corpus, in particular, is vulnerable to adversarial attacks such as corpus poisoning [70] and prompt injection
notes: Consequence changed from goal-hijack: ReliabilityRAG's metric is robust answer accuracy (and long-form generation quality) when a bounded number of retrieved web documents are corrupted, i.e. the attacker's win is a wrong final answer the user cannot distinguish. Provable robustness via Maximum Independent Set over a contradiction graph.

title: Tug-of-War between Knowledge: Exploring and Resolving Knowledge Conflicts in Retrieval-Augmented Language Models
evidence_quote: stronger RALMs emerge with the Dunning-Kruger effect, persistently favoring their faulty internal memory even when correct evidence is provided.
notes: Non-adversarial: conflicts between parametric memory and truthful/irrelevant/misleading retrieved evidence. Harm is a wrong final QA answer. 'Misleading evidence' is author-constructed but models no attacker.

title: Detecting Prompt Injection Attacks Against Application Using Classifiers
evidence_quote: injecting harmful content into the initial prompt provided to LLMs, with the intention of influencing their generated output. This manipulation can lead to biased, misleading, or even harmful responses
notes: Classifier-based detector (LSTM/FNN/RF/NB) trained on HackAPrompt-Playground-Submissions, which are user-submitted direct injections against web apps with predefined system prompts. Short paper; consequence is inferred from the dataset's goal-hijacking character rather than a stated harm metric.

title: Overcoming the Retrieval Barrier: Indirect Prompt Injection in the Wild for LLM Systems
evidence_quote: IPIs poison external data sources with hidden instructions that the LLM later retrieves and executes [36]. Once surfaced, these instructions can silently redirect system behavior, often in ways invisible to end users.
notes: The contribution is solving retrieval itself (a trigger fragment guaranteeing near-100% retrieval across 11 benchmarks and 8 embedding models), so the retriever channel is central rather than incidental. Spans RAG and agentic systems with diverse attack objectives, one of which (EchoLeak-style) is exfiltration.

title: Agent Data Injection Attacks are Realistic Threats to AI Agents
evidence_quote: ADI injects malicious data disguised as trusted data, such as security-critical metadata (e.g., resource identifiers or data origins) or agent context data (e.g., tool call and response formats). As a result, agents unknowingly execute unintended actions based on attacker-controlled data.
notes: Applied the route rule deliberately: the payload MASQUERADES as trusted metadata or tool-call formatting, but it physically arrives inside attacker-controlled external data the agent reads (comment bodies, web UI content, repo files), so the channel is tool-output rather than tool-metadata. Demonstrated arbitrary clicks on web agents and RCE/supply-chain on coding agents.

title: MIPIAD: Multilingual Indirect Prompt Injection Attack Defense with Qwen - TF-IDF Hybrid and Meta-Ensemble Learning
evidence_quote: The harder case is indirect prompt injection, where malicious instructions are hidden inside retrieved documents, emails, tables, web pages, or code rather than in the user's query
notes: Detector trained on 1.43M synthetic samples from BIPIA templates over five task families (email, table, QA, abstract, code). Channel is genuinely split between tool-output (email/table/code the model is given) and RAG (retrieved web/QA passages); the paper itself says 'retrieval-augmented and tool-using'. Consequence inferred from the stated injection goals (ignore user intent, expose information, unsafe tool actions), not measured.

title: Evaluating Long-Horizon Memory for Multi-Party Collaborative Dialogues
evidence_quote: multi-hop reasoning collapses under multi-party attribution even with oracle evidence (26% accuracy), temporal reasoning fails without explicit version semantics beyond timestamps, and memory awareness is bottlenecked by retrieval
notes: Consequence changed from reasoning-corruption to match the rule applied across this batch: EverMemBench scores 2,400 QA pairs, i.e. final answers under incomplete or stale multi-party memory. A validator could reasonably read 'multi-hop reasoning collapses' as intermediate degradation.

title: MELON: Provable Defense Against Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks in AI Agents
evidence_quote: Their access is limited to manipulating the external information retrieved by the agent via tool calls, such as websites, emails, or files. The attackers aim to redirect the agent from executing the original user task to performing a malicious task
notes: Defense evaluated on AgentDojo with ASR and utility-under-attack. Unambiguous on both axes.

title: ASPI: Seeking Ambiguity Clarification Amplifies Prompt Injection Vulnerability in LLM Agents
evidence_quote: When an agent solicits additional input from the user, it introduces a new channel through which external content enters the agent's context, one that is distinct from the tool-output channels examined in prior prompt-injection research
notes: Channel changed from tool-output: the paper's whole contribution is that the agent-solicited clarification reply is a DISTINCT channel from tool output; the tool-output condition is the matched control (1.8% ASR for o3 vs 34.0% in the clarification state). Coded direct-input because the payload arrives as user-supplied input the agent asked for.

title: United Minds or Isolated Agents? Exploring Coordination of LLMs under Cognitive Load Theory
evidence_quote: practitioners increasingly rely on heavy context engineering—curating intricate instructions, tool schemas, and multi-turn histories—the processing demands often exceed the LLM's effective attention budget, leading to context rot
notes: Channel changed from multi-agent: multi-agent (CoThinker) is the proposed REMEDY, while the degradation studied is context rot inside one over-packed context window. That packed context mixes direct-input (system instructions, few-shot demos), tool-metadata (tool schemas) and memory (multi-turn histories), so the single-channel pick is weak. Gains concentrate on reasoning-heavy tasks, hence reasoning-corruption.

title: End-to-End Context Compression at Scale
evidence_quote: Even when inputs fit within the model's maximum context window, models often struggle to reliably use information distributed across long contexts (Liu et al., 2024b; An et al., 2025). As a result, context and memory management have emerged as critical systems and modeling challenges
notes: Primarily a systems/efficiency paper (encoder-decoder KV-cache compression at 1:4/1:8/1:16). Two candidate harms: compression degrading answer quality (coded silent-corruption) and the KV-cache memory bottleneck itself (availability-loss). Coded by what is measured - general-task accuracy on the Pareto frontier - but this is a weak fit for a context-integrity consequence at all.

title: Verifying Intent and Harm: A Unified Defense Against LLM-Generated Threats
evidence_quote: many real-world attacks exploit a separation between adversarial intent expressed in the prompt and actionable harm manifested only in the response. As a result, prompt-only and response-only defenses frequently miss unsafe interactions that appear benign when viewed from either side in isolation.
notes: Channel changed from tool-output: the defense jointly verifies the USER PROMPT's intent and the response's harm, and all five threat categories are driven by adversarial users interacting directly with the model. Consequence is the model producing attacker-desired policy-violating output.

title: TSUBASA: Improving Long-Horizon Personalization via Evolving Memory and Self-Learning with Context Distillation
evidence_quote: standard episodic memory systems often act as linear-growing vector databases (Lewis et al., 2020; Madaan et al., 2022), failing on "reflective" tasks that require implicit temporal reasoning across interactions
notes: Consequence changed from reasoning-corruption: TSUBASA is evaluated on LoCoMo and LongMemEval, i.e. answer accuracy under evolving/stale personal memory, so the measured harm is a wrong final answer. 'Reflective tasks requiring implicit temporal reasoning' could support the reasoning-corruption reading.

title: A Security Analysis of the OpenClaw AI Agent Framework
evidence_quote: a malicious skill distributed through the plugin channel [13] executed a two-stage dropper entirely within the LLM context, bypassing the exec pipeline entirely and illustrating that the skill distribution surface constitutes an attack vector outside any runtime policy primitive
notes: Taxonomy of 470 OpenClaw advisories spanning many layers (exec policy, gateway, channel adapters, sandbox, browser, plugin/skill, agent/prompt) and many techniques (identity spoofing, policy bypass, cross-layer composition, prompt injection, supply-chain trust escalation). Only the third principal finding is about content entering the LLM context, so I coded that one; supply-chain and tool-output are both defensible. Most of the corpus is framework vulnerabilities rather than context-channel issues.

title: ’Ignore All and Accept My Resume’: The Impact of Prompt Injection in Automatic Resume Screening
evidence_quote: In the context of resume screening, job candidates often exploit this technique to manipulate the applicant tracking system (ATS) by inserting a harmful prompt into the resume to be approved.
notes: Short review, not an experimental study. The resume is placed into the prompt by the ATS (an upstream service), hence direct-input. Consequence is a judgement call: the screener still performs screening but obeys the candidate's embedded instruction to approve, which reads as goal-hijack; a validator could code the wrong hire/reject verdict as silent-corruption.

title: Visual and Structural Prompt Injection in Medical Rag Systems: a Comparative Robustness Analysis
evidence_quote: the objective was to have the model diagnose a false septic shock and prescribe meropenem, a high-risk antibiotic with no clinical indication, by suppressing a stable patient profile (context suppression)
notes: Channel changed from cross-modal by the route rule: the payloads are FORMATTED visually (white text, micro-typography, metadata), but they live in clinical discharge summaries that the RAG parser ingests and the retriever surfaces - the route is RAG, the format is visual. Consequence changed from goal-hijack: the model still performs diagnosis and produces a wrong clinical conclusion that nothing flags (average ASR 47.78%; Gemma-3 96.33%, Meditron-7B 8.67%).

title: Memory in the LLM Era: Modular Architectures and Strategies in a Unified Framework
evidence_quote: Under this framework, we compare representative methods on two typical long-term conversational benchmarks, LOCOMO [57] and LONGMEMEVAL [91]. Beyond overall performance, we analyze practical robustness dimensions, including context scalability and positional sensitivity.
notes: Experiment/analysis/benchmark paper unifying agent memory methods into four stages. Consequence changed from reasoning-corruption for consistency with the other LoCoMo/LongMemEval papers in this batch: the metric is final QA accuracy under compressed or incomplete memory. Their Figure 1 also flags naive long-context prompting as hitting 'context overflow', an availability-loss framing.

title: SAFARI: Scaling Long Horizon Agentic Fault Attribution via Active Investigation
evidence_quote: Current methods for effectively diagnosing agent failures load the full trajectory into an LLM's context window, which suffers from attention dilution and fails when agentic traces inevitably exceed context limits.
notes: Consequence changed from reasoning-corruption: the stated problem is that multi-million-token traces exceed every context window, and SAFARI 'maintains a 0.58 precision even when the target fault resides 5x beyond the model's native context window, a scenario where traditional evaluators fail entirely'. Channel kept as direct-input because the baseline loads the trajectory straight into the prompt; SAFARI's own design reads it back through tools, so tool-output is arguable.

title: SUGAR: Leveraging Contextual Confidence for Smarter Retrieval
evidence_quote: LLMs get easily distracted by noisy retrieved documents and generate seemingly plausible, but incorrect outputs, even though the parametric knowledge of the model would have been enough to accurately answer the question, had retrieval not been triggered.
notes: Adaptive-retrieval method using semantic uncertainty to decide whether to retrieve. No adversary; harm is a plausible-but-wrong QA answer caused by irrelevant or factually incorrect retrieved passages.

title: A Critical Evaluation of Defenses against Prompt Injection Attacks: [Dataset/Tool Paper]
evidence_quote: A prompt injection attack involves crafting and embedding such an injected prompt into the data so that, when the LLM processes the instruction + contaminated data, it performs an attacker-chosen task rather than the intended task.
notes: Channel changed from tool-output: PIEval evaluates the abstract instruction+contaminated-data setting on text tasks (summarization, sentiment, spam, NLI), where the untrusted data is concatenated into the prompt by the application rather than returned by a tool. The intro also names tool-description injection (tool-metadata) as a motivating case, so the setting is deliberately channel-agnostic. Consequence is unambiguous.

title: FinVault: Benchmarking Financial Agent Safety in Execution-Grounded Environments
evidence_quote: we categorize the attacks into three groups. (i) Prompt injection attacks, which include Direct JSON Injection and Instruction Overriding (Greshake et al., 2023; Zhan et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024a); (ii) Jailbreaking attacks, encompassing Role Playing, Progressive Prompting
notes: Both axes changed. Channel: every implemented attack technique is delivered by the adversary interacting with the agent (JSON injection, instruction overriding, role play, authority impersonation), e.g. 'the attacker requests splitting a $50,000 transfer into ten $5,000 transactions', so direct-input, not tool-output. Consequence: the 107 vulnerabilities are compliance violations (35%), fraudulent approvals (28%), privilege escalation (18%), information leakage (12%), audit evasion (7%) - unauthorized state-changing actions, i.e. goal-hijack. Unauthorized remittances do move the victim's money, so resource-abuse is arguable.

title: MGA: Memory-Driven GUI Agent for Observation-Centric Interaction
evidence_quote: long-horizon automation remains constrained by two critical bottlenecks: context overload from raw sequential trajectory dependence
notes: GUI agent; the degrading content is the agent's own accumulated visual-textual interaction history, which MGA replaces with a structured state-delta memory. Harm is error cascades and 'irrelevant historical interference' across decision steps, evaluated as OSWorld task success, hence intermediate decisions. 'Context overload' is also named, so availability-loss is a secondary reading. Observations are screenshots, so cross-modal is an arguable channel.

title: Multilingual Hidden Prompt Injection Attacks on LLM-Based Academic Reviewing
evidence_quote: We find that prompt injection induces substantial changes in review scores and accept/reject decisions for English, Japanese, and Chinese injections, while Arabic injections produce little to no effect.
notes: ~500 real ICML papers with hidden instructions in four languages, reviewed by an LLM. Channel: the paper document is handed to the reviewer model as the data to review (direct-input via an upstream pipeline); cross-modal is arguable since the payload is hidden in the PDF rendering. Consequence is genuinely contested: the model still performs reviewing but is steered to the author's desired verdict - coded goal-hijack for instruction-following, but silent-corruption (a wrong final decision with a HIDDEN cause) is at least as defensible.

title: MPIB: A Benchmark for Medical Prompt Injection Attacks and Clinical Safety in LLMs
evidence_quote: MPIB emphasizes outcome-level risk via the Clinical Harm Event Rate (CHER), which measures high-severity clinical harm events under a clinically grounded taxonomy, and reports CHER alongside Attack Success Rate (ASR) to disentangle instruction compliance from downstream patient risk.
notes: Consequence changed from goal-hijack: the benchmark deliberately separates instruction compliance (ASR = goal-hijack) from the clinically unsafe OUTPUT (CHER), emphasises CHER, and finds the two diverge substantially. Channel: covers both direct and RAG-mediated injection and reports that robustness depends on which, but the indirect RAG variant is the paper's stated concern.

title: Multi-Criteria Evaluation of Large Language Models (LLMs): Balancing Performance and Security
evidence_quote: Without appropriate safeguards, the use of LLMs-whether for internal systems or customer-facing applications-may expose organizations to prompt injection, data poisoning, denial of service, and jailbreak attacks, many of which are listed in the OWASP Top 10 for LLM applications [6].
notes: An AHP multi-criteria decision method for choosing an LLM, scoring task efficiency against vulnerability-scanner results. Barely a context-integrity paper: the security axis is a black-box scanner firing injection/jailbreak prompts at the model (direct-input) and the consequence is inferred, not measured. Denial of service is among the listed risks, so availability-loss also appears in its risk list.

title: ObliInjection: Order-Oblivious Prompt Injection Attack to LLM Agents with Multi-source Data
evidence_quote: We consider three categories of target tasks: review summarization, news summarization, and RAG-based question answering. For each category, we adopt a widely used dataset: Amazon Reviews, Multi-News, and HotpotQA.
notes: Deliberately channel-agnostic: the paper's framing spans review segments, news articles, RAG passages and MCP tool name-description pairs (tool-metadata), and the attack's novelty is being oblivious to segment ORDER, not to channel. Coded direct-input because two of the three evaluated datasets are multi-document summarization where the application concatenates supplied segments into the prompt; the third (HotpotQA) is RAG. Consequence is unambiguous: an attacker-chosen task replaces the intended one, ASR near 100%.

title: ARC: Active and Reflection-driven Context Management for Long-Horizon Information Seeking Agents
evidence_quote: Once compressed, early errors, outdated assumptions, or misaligned emphasis are difficult to correct, as prior summaries are rarely revisited.
notes: Channel changed from direct-input: the degrading content is the agent's own accumulated reasoning, actions and observations, which ARC actively reorganises. Consequence kept as reasoning-corruption because the paper's stated failure is loss of a coherent internal reasoning STATE across steps, though the headline metric is final accuracy on BrowseComp-ZH (+11%), which would support silent-corruption.

title: Prompt Overflow: What the Guardrail Inspects Is Not What the Model Infers
evidence_quote: We introduce a novel Prompt Overflow Attack, which exploits this mismatch by fragmenting malicious instructions and interleaving them with benign filler content across an overlong prompt, such that no individual inspected segment appears malicious
notes: Channel changed from tool-output: the attack is carried in the user prompt that the guardrail screens (e.g. Llama Prompt Guard 2's 512-token window) before it reaches a long-context LLM. Novel vector - the vulnerability is the context-window MISMATCH between guardrail and model, not the payload's semantics. Consequence is the downstream model reassembling and executing the attacker's instruction.

title: Token-Efficient Prompt Injection Attack: Provoking Cessation in LLM Reasoning via Adaptive Token Compression
evidence_quote: the reasoning process can be completely interrupted, resulting in no final answer being produced
notes: Attacker-crafted arithmetic reasoning tokens are appended to the application's prompt; the measured outcome is an empty API response (thinking stopped), i.e. the model cannot finish and nobody gains - availability-loss, not corrupted reasoning. Channel: the payload reaches the model as text in the final prompt of an LLM-integrated app.

title: The Promptware Kill Chain: How Prompt Injections Gradually Evolved Into a Multistep Malware Delivery Mechanism
evidence_quote: Exfiltration is the most common action on objective. A recurring pattern in enterprise-targeted incidents is LLM-assisted exfiltration, in which the LLM reads sensitive data and encodes it into output that bypasses organizational exfiltration controls.
notes: Seven-stage kill-chain survey of 36 incidents spanning web pages, images, memory and retrieval poisoning, C2 and agent-to-agent spread, so no single channel applies. Consequence is also multi-stage, but the paper measures the end objective across its corpus and reports exfiltration as the most common; persistence is a stage, not the terminal outcome.

title: CodeDelegator: Mitigating Context Pollution via Role Separation in Code-as-Action Agents
evidence_quote: Using a single agent for both leads to context pollution from debugging traces and intermediate failures, impairing long-horizon performance.
notes: No adversary: pollution is self-inflicted by the agent's own code-execution traces, which arrive as observations from the executed code (tool-output), not from the user prompt. What degrades is planning and sub-task dispatch - intermediate decisions - so reasoning-corruption; task-success numbers on tau2-bench/MCPMark are the symptom, not a silently wrong answer.

title: MCP-Guard: A Multi-Stage Defense-in-Depth Framework for Securing Model Context Protocol in Agentic AI
evidence_quote: Tool Poisoning embeds malicious instructions in tool descriptions to hijack intent (e.g., a benign calculator exfiltrating SSH keys)
notes: MCP defense; MCP-AttackBench payloads are embedded into valid MCP fields (description, inputSchema) read before invocation, so tool-metadata. Consequence is a dominance call: the headline scenario is key exfiltration, but the framing throughout is hijacking agent intent/control flow via poisoned tool definitions.

title: ALCUNA: Large Language Models Meet New Knowledge
evidence_quote: For experiments in the zero-shot setting, our inputs are structured representations of new knowledge and questions to be answered by the model.
notes: No adversary - artificial entities are benign but conflict with parametric knowledge. The new knowledge is placed directly in the prompt as a structured representation; no retriever is involved, so not RAG (retrieval is only motivation). Measured by answer accuracy on MC/fill-in-the-blank/Boolean questions: wrong final answers with no signal.

title: Attention is All You Need to Defend Against Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks in LLMs
evidence_quote: An adversary injects adversarial instructions into external data sources to goal-hijack the LLM-integrated application.
notes: IPI defense (RENNERVATE). Problem is formulated over 'the external data X retrieved according to the user instruction' - retrieved passages, so RAG rather than a tool return; the FIPI/unseen datasets are NLP task data blocks in the retrieved-data slot. ASR of the injected task is the metric, so goal-hijack.

title: Dynamic Parametric Retrieval Augmented Generation for Test-time Knowledge Enhancement
evidence_quote: when the internal knowledge of LLMs conflicts with the external context, a phenomenon known as RAG hallucination (or knowledge conflict) arises, causing LLMs to produce incorrect answers even when accurate documents are provided
notes: Non-adversarial RAG knowledge conflict; retrieved Wikipedia documents. Measured on QA accuracy - wrong final answers with nothing signalling it. Labels unchanged.

title: The Landscape of Prompt Injection Threats in LLM Agents: From Taxonomy to Analysis
evidence_quote: the LLM agents are vulnerable to Prompt Injection (PI) attacks, in which untrusted inputs manipulate the backbone LLM's output to hijack the agent behavior
notes: SoK plus the AgentPI benchmark. The SoK half spans several channels, but the paper's own contribution evaluates context-dependent agent tasks where payloads sit in runtime environmental observations (config files, tool returns), so tool-output carries it. ASR of hijacked agent behaviour is the headline metric.

title: BinaryShield: Cross-Service Threat Intelligence in LLM Services using Privacy-Preserving Fingerprints
evidence_quote: We evaluate BinaryShield using the recent prompt injection dataset from [17], which contains real-world attack and benign prompts.
notes: Cross-service threat-intelligence sharing over fingerprints of suspicious prompts submitted to LLM services; the corpus is user-submitted attack prompts, so direct-input rather than tool returns. Consequence is generic prompt-injection hijacking of the service; the paper measures detection F1, not a specific harm, hence medium.

title: The Task Shield: Enforcing Task Alignment to Defend Against Indirect Prompt Injection in LLM Agents
evidence_quote: attackers embed malicious prompts within external data sources (environment), such as documents, web pages, or tool output, that LLM agents process
notes: AgentDojo-based IPI defense; injections live in tool returns the agent reads mid-task, and the metric is attack success rate for the injected goal versus task utility. Labels unchanged.

title: Prompt Injection Attacks on Agentic Coding Assistants: A Systematic Analysis of Vulnerabilities in Skills, Tools, and Protocol Ecosystems
evidence_quote: attacks where malicious instructions embedded in external content manipulate agent behavior
notes: SoK of 78 studies with an explicitly three-dimensional taxonomy whose delivery-vector axis spans direct input, repository/docs/web content, MCP protocol metadata, skills and multimodal payloads - no single channel dominates, so none. Consequence also spans exfiltration, persistence and viral spread; goal-hijack is the common entry outcome, hence low confidence.
